title: The Burdah
hookLine: al-Busiri's poem of the cloak, praising the Prophet ﷺ, sung across the world

cards: A poet lies in bed in Egypt, half his body unable to move. That's how the story people tell about Sharaf al-Din al-Busiri begins.
With nothing left to him but words, he composes a long poem praising the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and recites it, weeping, over and over.

One night he dreams the Prophet stands beside him, passes his hand over him, and lays his cloak, his burdah, across his body. In the morning, the story says, al-Busiri gets up and walks out of the house.

teach.h: A POEM NAMED FOR A CLOAK.
teach.b: Whether someone hears that healing as a miracle, a blessing or a story, the poem itself is real, and it traveled. People simply call it the Burdah, the poem of the cloak.

It opens the old way Arabic poems opened, with longing: a lover remembering a place and a neighbor, unable to stop his tears. Then it turns. The poet confesses his own faults and warns his soul against its appetites.
Then he pours out praise: the Prophet's birth, his night journey, his patience, his mercy.
Every line ends on the same rhyme, the letter mim, so the whole poem rings like one long bell. And people sang it.

Across Egypt, Turkey, North and East Africa, South and Southeast Asia, groups gather to sing it together, often with a refrain between verses, often around the Prophet's birthday. Why praise the Prophet in poetry at all?
Those who love the Burdah point to a verse of the Qur'an.

In Pickthall's translation: "Lo! Allah and His angels shower blessings on the Prophet. O ye who believe! Ask blessings on him and salute him with a worthy salutation." A poem like this is one way of answering that.
Not every Muslim sings it. Some scholars, especially in reform movements, have objected to a few of its lines, saying they ask of the Prophet what only God can give.
Those who love the poem read the same lines as asking for his intercession, which they believe God grants. Both sides would say they are guarding the Prophet's honor.
And the poem keeps being sung.

how: In Egypt, Turkey, North and East Africa and South and Southeast Asia, groups gather to sing the Burdah, often around the Prophet's birthday; other Muslims, following reformist scholars, do not recite it or object to some of its lines.

games.q: you're al-Busiri: half your body won't move, and all you have left is words. what do you do with them?
o: compose a poem in praise of the Prophet.
games.why: the story says he composed the Burdah, dreamed the Prophet laid his cloak over him, and woke able to walk. a story people tell; the poem is real.

practice: Play the opening of a recording of the Burdah if you can, or hum a soft mmm on each out-breath, like its one rhyme, and listen to how the voices repeat and the refrain comes back around.
If you pray, you can send blessings on the Prophet with the words Muslims use, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam; if you don't, simply listen to people praising someone they love.

wordCard.voice: The Burdah. Al-Busiri's poem of the cloak, praising the Prophet, every line rhymed on one letter, sung in many lands. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a cloak or mantle; the name people give al-Busiri's poem.
